title: Tuples
description: A tuple is a list whose values are locked the moment you make it.

content.value: A list is built to be changed. Sometimes that is exactly wrong. The days of the week, the three numbers of a colour, a fixed pair of map coordinates: none of those should ever gain an extra item halfway through your program. For values like that, Python has the tuple.

You make a tuple with round parentheses instead of square brackets. Everything you already know about reading a list still applies: index from 0, count backwards with negative numbers, measure it with `len()`, and loop over it with `for`.

months = ("January", "February", "March")

print(months[0])      # January
print(months[-1])     # March
print(len(months))    # 3

for month in months:
    print(month)

The one thing you cannot do is change it. There is no `.append()` on a tuple, and assigning to an index raises a `TypeError`. Switch the lab below over to tuple and try the buttons to see Python refuse.

coords = (10, 20)

# Both of these would stop the program with an error:
# coords[0] = 5
# coords.append(30)

print(coords)

That refusal is the feature, not a limitation. If a value is never meant to move, a tuple makes accidentally moving it impossible instead of merely unlikely, and anyone reading your code can see at a glance that it is fixed.

The question to ask is simple: will this collection grow, shrink or change while the program runs? A shopping list, a score history and a bag of collected items all change, so they are lists. A date, a coordinate pair and a set of fixed options do not, so they are tuples.
A one item tuple needs a trailing comma: `(5,)` is a tuple, while `(5)` is just the number 5 with brackets around it. This one catches almost everybody once.

quiz.question: Which brackets make a tuple?
quiz.explain: Tuples use parentheses. Square brackets make lists and curly brackets make dictionaries.

quiz.question: What happens when you run  colors = ("red", "blue")  then  colors.append("green")?
options: The tuple gains a third item
Python raises an error, because a tuple cannot be changed
The tuple turns into a list
quiz.explain: A tuple has no .append() at all, so Python stops with an AttributeError. That protection is the whole reason to pick a tuple.

quiz.question: Which of these is the better job for a tuple?
options: A shopping list you keep adding to
The fixed pair of numbers giving a treasure's location
The names of players who have joined a game so far
A queue of jobs waiting to be done
quiz.explain: The other three all grow or shrink while the program runs, so they need lists. A fixed location never changes, so locking it is helpful.
